column3: Directly parallels worldly life being made attractive and reverses its status at the Resurrection.
Life, death, and return place worldly life within an inescapable return to God.
Shows Satan making prior peoples' deeds attractive, exposing a corrupt source of embellishment.
Expands worldly life into play, adornment, boasting, and rivalry in wealth and children, then shows its decay.
Immediately contrasts the listed attractions with a better abiding return for the mindful.
Uses adornment for the nearest heaven, distinguishing created beauty from the human desire inventory.
Names gold and silver and condemns their hoarding rather than their use.
Supplies obedience to God and the Messenger as the local alternative to turning away.
Calls evil deeds made attractive, linking embellishment with distortion and disbelief.
Calls worldly luxury mere enjoyment and reserves the Hereafter for the mindful.
The sequence of life, death, and revival relativizes present life.
Pharaoh's evil work is made attractive and turns him from the way.
Identifies horses as both riding provision and adornment, clarifying one item in the inventory.
Reorients love toward God through following the Messenger.
Uses adornment for the sky before observers, a distinct divine use of beauty.
Counters self-exalting possession with worship, kindness, and rejection of pride.
Night and day entering one another do not illuminate the desire inventory.
Calls what is on earth its adornment and makes it a test of better action.
Contrasts temporary worldly enjoyment with a good promise that will be met.
God's living, sustaining reality supplies a remote contrast to transient worldly goods.
Satan makes deeds attractive and thereby bars people from the way despite insight.
Earthly ornament and its produce suddenly become harvested ruin, sharpening the transience of worldly enjoyment.
The cosmic alternation of night and day does not add to the desire inventory.
Names Satan's making their deeds attractive alongside hardened hearts.
Adornment and usable goods yield passing foam, while what benefits people remains.
God reverses life and death and gives provision without reckoning, widening the verse's ending.
Those denying the Hereafter have their deeds made attractive and wander blindly.
Explicitly calls worldly life temporary enjoyment and the Hereafter the lasting abode.
God gives life, causes death, and inherits, placing possessions under divine final ownership.
Satan makes idolatrous practice attractive and blocks guidance.
The listed people, beasts, and livestock lead to reverent knowledge rather than acquisitive display.
Its account before God supplies a nearby but indirect horizon for the contrast in 3:14.
Companions make what is before and behind attractive, ending in loss.
Pairs and livestock are created as means of riding, framing items in 3:14 as bestowed utilities.
The stripping of daylight from night does not clarify worldly desire.
Directly depicts evil work appearing good to its doer.
Wealth and children are a trial, while God holds the great reward.
Calling to good and forbidding wrong provides only a general ethical counterpoint.
Adorning the nearest heaven with lamps is a separate cosmic use of adornment.
Agriculture and livestock become objects of false allocation, warning against corrupted handling of listed goods.
Divine knowledge of cosmic movements does not add to 3:14's desire inventory.
Satan makes deeds attractive before abandoning those who trusted his assurance.
God's reward and best recompense directly reinforce that the best return is with Him.
Piety is loved by God, supplying the quality that receives the better return in the next verse.
Contrasts revived, illuminated life with deeds made attractive to disbelievers.
Following desires after neglecting prayer ends in error.
The ordered sun, moon, night, and day do not clarify the worldly goods named in 3:14.
Partners make the killing of children attractive, showing embellishment can conceal devastating wrongdoing.
Love of worldly good can distract from remembrance of the Lord.
Revelation in truth is a remote corrective, not a direct treatment of desire.
Satan explicitly vows to make things attractive on earth and lead people astray.
Its required provision in divorce concerns women but adds little to desire as worldly enjoyment.
The presentation of every deed warns that present attraction does not escape final exposure.
A ruinous assumption is made attractive in hearts, tying adornment to inner deception.
Followers of desires seek to turn others far away.
God gives and removes dominion, undercutting reliance on worldly status and control.
Every community's deed is made attractive, yet all return to God for disclosure.
Livestock provide warmth, benefits, and food, framing one listed possession as provision.
Gold and what souls desire appear in an abiding garden, contrasting enduring fulfillment with worldly enjoyment.
The disbelievers' scheming is made attractive and bars them from the way.
Names desire directed away from women as excess, marking desire as morally accountable.
Its warning against obedience that returns believers to disbelief is only indirectly related.
Sets clear proof against evil work made attractive and following desires.
Repeats desire directed away from women and calls it ignorance.
Cosmic creation and movement do not clarify the attraction of worldly goods.
Shows a positive counterpart: faith made beloved and adorned in hearts, with disbelief made hateful.
Nearness and a good return with God echo the verse's better destination.
The refusal of judgment by the Book does not add to the desire inventory.
Marriage regulation mentions women but does not treat them as worldly attraction.
A broken good promise and feared anger offer only a distant contrast.
A statement about unrepaid favor does not clarify 3:14.
Persistent disbelief after faith does not add to worldly desire or adornment.
An everlasting great reward with God reinforces the better return beyond worldly enjoyment.
Commands temporary enjoyment before eventual knowledge, stressing its limited horizon.
The covenant's ethical commands do not directly illuminate the desire inventory.
Trading revealed truth for a small price warns against valuing a worldly exchange over what is higher.
Its divorce protections do not address desire as worldly adornment.
Mercy, consultation, and reliance do not materially clarify 3:14.
Forbids proud, boastful conduct, a response to the status seeking in worldly goods.
Provision from God without reckoning reinforces the verse's turn from stockpiled goods to divine giving.
Forbids exulting over what one receives and condemns pride.
The qintar is an ethical trust, not simply an object of attraction.
Mentions sons and women under oppression, not as the goods of 3:14.
A qintar in marital dealings is protected from unjust recovery, limiting its treatment as mere wealth.
The rejection of deifying Jesus and his mother does not clarify worldly desire.
Explicitly calls wealth and sons worldly adornment and ranks lasting righteous deeds higher.
Affirms God's adornment and good provision while locating their full purity at the Resurrection.
Loss of wealth, lives, and fruits is a test, challenging attachment to the listed goods.
Explicitly calls all given things worldly enjoyment and adornment, while God's possession is better and more lasting.
The contrast of daughters and sons is polemical and only shares a family term.
Cultivated produce and fruits are signs from God, reframing agricultural abundance as evidence.
Gardens, fruit, purified spouses, and abiding life form an enduring counterpart to the worldly list.
The change of direction in prayer does not clarify worldly attractions.
God's ownership of all heavens and earth gives a broad, indirect check on possessiveness.
The opening of Solomon's letter does not add to 3:14.
Fasting rules do not clarify the listed worldly attractions.
God's expansion and restriction of provision gives only a broad context for wealth.
The command to fear God and obey does not add specific understanding of 3:14.
Exclusive worship is not a direct treatment of worldly desire here.
The offer of daughters in this narrative does not clarify the desire inventory.
Shows the insufficiency of seeking only a worldly portion rather than an ultimate share.
Pairs a good worldly portion with a good final portion, preventing a purely worldly horizon.
Explicitly calls worldly life the enjoyment of delusion after death and recompense are stated.
Warns against being deceived by disbelievers' movement through the land.
Calls that apparent prosperity a small enjoyment before a grievous destination.
Restrains coveting what God has apportioned to others and redirects desire to His bounty.
Calls worldly enjoyment little when set beside the Hereafter.
Places the reward of both this world and the Hereafter with God.
Forbids treating God's good things as prohibited, balancing 3:14's warning against attachment.
Defines worldly life as play and amusement and prefers the final abode for the mindful.
Warns that worldly life can deceive and that a soul may be destroyed by what it earned.
Frames cultivated produce and livestock under divine giving and forbids waste.
Describes livestock as carrying and slaughter stock, framing them as provision under God's name.
Commands taking adornment and eating without excess, regulating rather than rejecting adornment.
Describes those deceived by worldly life after making religion amusement and play.
Links clinging to earth with following desire and losing guidance.
Explicitly calls wealth and children a trial and locates great reward with God.
Contrasts seeking the immediate gain of this world with God's intent for the Hereafter.
Lists family, wealth, trade, and dwellings as beloved attachments that must not outrank God and His cause.
Calls the enjoyment of worldly life little beside the Hereafter.
Wealth and children are not signs of favor but a means of affliction in worldly life.
Depicts prior peoples enjoying their share and becoming absorbed in vain discourse.
Again treats wealth and children as a worldly affliction rather than a final good.
Those content with worldly life and reassured by it are heedless of God's signs.
Names worldly enjoyment as a temporary benefit before human wrongdoing returns upon itself.
Calls their worldly gain brief before return to God.
Calls Pharaoh's wealth and adornment a means by which people are led from God's way.
Those seeking worldly life and its adornment receive their works here but lose the Hereafter.
People rejoice in worldly life although it is only a brief enjoyment beside the Hereafter.
Identifies preference for worldly life over the Hereafter as a mark of far error.
Connects rain to drink, grazing, and vegetation, placing agricultural goods within divine provision.
Names crops, olives, palms, grapes, and fruits as signs to be reflected on.
Names jewelry drawn from the sea, another instance of adornment as divine provision.
Directly identifies preferring worldly life to the Hereafter.
Calls their enjoyment little before painful punishment.
Whoever seeks the immediate receives a limited allotted portion before a blameworthy end.
All receive from their Lord's gift, so worldly allotment is not self-secured.
Shows that worldly degrees vary while the Hereafter has greater degrees and distinction.
Satan's promised share in wealth and children exposes them as a field of deception.
Forbids following one whose heart follows desire and whose affair is excess.
The parable of two gardens tests the reading of cultivated wealth as security.
The destruction of garden produce makes visible the fragility of accumulated worldly goods.
Forbids extending the eyes toward worldly splendor given as a test; God's provision is better and more lasting.
The wealthy leaders appeal to worldly life, wealth, and children to reject resurrection.
Questions whether wealth and children should be read as hastening good to their possessors.
Denies that added wealth and children prove an early bestowal of good.
Treats worldly gain as transient, even where sexual exploitation is sought for it.
Praises those whom trade and sale do not distract from God's remembrance.
Declares that wealth and sons will not benefit on the decisive day.
Questions the value of years of continued enjoyment before the threatened reality arrives.
Qarun's immense store of wealth becomes a case against exultant self-reliance.
Commands seeking the final abode through what God has given without forgetting one's worldly share.
Shows onlookers wishing for Qarun's worldly portion because of its apparent fortune.
Those given knowledge answer that God's reward is better for faith and right action.
Explicitly calls worldly life amusement and play, while true life belongs to the final abode.
Critiques knowing only the outward aspect of worldly life while being heedless of the Hereafter.
Warns against being deceived by worldly life and by the deceiver concerning God.
Addresses the desire for worldly life and its adornment in contrast with choosing God and the final abode.
Treats women's beauty as an attraction that cannot override a stated divine limit.
Rejects wealth and children as proof of greater honor or immunity.
States that wealth and children do not bring people near to God except through faith and right action.
Warns all people not to let worldly life deceive them concerning God.
Contrasts cultivation for the Hereafter with cultivation for this world and its limited yield.
Calls whatever is given worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more lasting.
Depicts abundant houses and elevated furnishings as worldly goods God could give disbelievers.
Continues the inventory of doors, couches, and furnishings as merely worldly provision.
Explains loss through treating God's signs as mockery and being deceived by worldly life.
Rebukes those who exhausted their good things and enjoyed them in worldly life.
Contrasts believers' gardens with disbelievers' unreflective worldly enjoyment.
Calls worldly life play and amusement and warns against attachment when wealth is demanded.
Links turning away from remembrance to desiring only worldly life.
Forbids wealth and children from distracting believers from God's remembrance.
Names preferring worldly life among the marks of exceeding limits.
Restraining the self from desire is paired with fear of standing before the Lord.
Explicitly names the preference for worldly life.
States that the Hereafter is better and more enduring.
Names an excessive love of wealth.
Explicitly describes intense love for wealth.
Rivalry in accumulation distracts until graves are reached.
